history.title: Leak Alert Schedule vs Owner Sensor Assembly

style_when: the news is structural and abstract — a stack reordered, a layer added, a flow rerouted — and there is no literal object that carries it, so the idea is stated as a small physical assembly of recognisable parts rather than as bare shapes
prompt: A matte clay 3D split-screen diptych on a textured concrete garage floor, a vertical seam separating left and right. Left half: a cylindrical water-meter housing with a fixed rotary cam wheel cut with twenty-four detents and one locked latch position. Right half: a small owner-run sensor module with an adjustable threshold lever and a short antenna nub. A galvanised steel pipe stub links the halves across the seam. Hard directional key light from the left rakes the assembly, throwing long contact shadows. Palette: bone white, graphite, deep pine green. No text, no numbers.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, numbers, watermarks, UI
rationale: The story is a structural contrast between two control regimes—a fixed utility cadence and an owner-adjustable sensor—with no single purchasable object carrying the whole thesis. A matte clay 3D mechanical assembly makes the two cadences legible as physical parts, and the split-screen framing enforces the duality.
cue: a notification schedule, not a detector
subject: a split-screen matte clay assembly of a utility water-meter housing with fixed 24-hour cam and an owner-run sensor module with adjustable threshold lever
core_thesis: A utility's smart-meter leak alert is a notification schedule, not a detector: the cadence belongs to the utility, and only an owner-run sensor lets you choose the interval and threshold that match what a leak costs.
core_conflict: The utility's fixed 24-hour-to-biweekly alert cadence leaves homeowners exposed for up to two weeks, while an owner-run sensor can be tuned to the precise interval and threshold a hidden slab leak actually demands.
composition: split-screen diptych, left-right scenario contrast: fixed utility interval cam vs owner-adjustable threshold sensor

review.depicts: Two matte clay objects on a concrete slab joined by a short metal pipe fitting: on the left a cream-coloured cylindrical meter housing with a recessed slotted dial face and a protruding tab, and on the right a green rectangular box topped with a small metal lever and a short nub.
review.reason: The frame's meter housing paired with a lever-adjustable module mirrors the article's contrast between the utility's fixed water-meter alert interval and an owner-run sensor with adjustable threshold, though the '24-hour cam' and dial numeracy are only implied rather than legible.
